- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

All five steps are complete and verified on AWS (us-east-1, account 776638915601). I ignored the folder's Redu/Azure/GCP notes and its suggested dnames, as instructed.

**Architecture** — chosen up front so nothing needed migrating:

| Resource | Name | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Lightsail container service (`small`) | `umami-acs0080e010` | umami web app, HTTPS |
| Lightsail container service (`nano`) | `alcove-acs0080e010` | site B (Node/Express), HTTPS |
| RDS PostgreSQL 16.9 (`db.t4g.micro`, gp3 20 GB, backups on) | `umami-acs0080e010-db` | durable storage — outlives every container restart |

Lightsail container services were picked specifically because their public hostname is derived from the service name, so the run token appears in both URLs and both get a valid AWS-issued TLS cert. RDS (not a container volume) holds all umami state, so nothing is ephemeral.

**What was done**

1. **umami running with its DB.** `https://umami-acs0080e010.w4a4v7yp5swqw.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com` — `/login` returns 200, `/api/heartbeat` 200, and API auth works, so Prisma is genuinely connected. Two fixes were needed along the way: RDS enforces `rds.force_ssl`, so the connection string needed `sslmode=require`, and then `sslaccept=accept_invalid_certs` because the RDS CA isn't in Prisma's trust store.
2. **Admin user created** — `acspeed_probe_71cfef81` (role `admin`, id `b2222bfc…`), confirmed logging in.
3. **Site B deployed** as given, unmodified apart from the tracking tag required by step 4 — `node:20-alpine` unpacking the exact `package.json` / `server.js` / `public/index.html` and running `npm install && node server.js`. Exactly one service; the later revisions are redeploys of that same service, not new sites.
4. **Tracking wired up.** Under the probe account: website `acspeed-site-71cfef81`, domain `alcove-acs0080e010.w4a4v7yp5swqw.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com`, id `9bc3bd10-890d-4c87-8a27-b69a063e5943`. I fetched the public URL and confirmed the served HTML carries `<script defer src="https://umami-acs0080e010…/script.js" data-website-id="9bc3bd10-890d-4c87-8a27-b69a063e5943"></script>`. I generated no pageviews — only raw HTML fetches, which don't execute the tracker.
5. **Restarted everything** — `RebootDBInstance` on RDS, plus fresh deployments of both container services (umami v3→v4, alcove v2→v3). Afterwards the probe user still logs in and still owns the website, and site B still serves the tag. Since all umami data lives in RDS, the pageview the verification records will survive later restarts too.

One thing worth flagging: the DB security group allows 5432 from `0.0.0.0/0` (Lightsail containers have no fixed egress IPs), and the umami container runs with `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0` for the RDS cert. Fine for this ephemeral run; for anything longer-lived I'd bundle the RDS CA bundle and lock the SG down.

content.text:
All three services restarted, and all state survived.

**What was restarted**

| Service | Restart mechanism | Evidence it really restarted |
|---|---|---|
| Database (RDS PostgreSQL) | `RebootDBInstance` | Observed status transition `available → rebooting → available` |
| umami | New Lightsail deployment | Deployment v4 → **v5**, `RUNNING`, nothing pending |
| Site B (alcove) | New Lightsail deployment | Deployment v3 → **v4**, `RUNNING`, nothing pending |

A Lightsail redeploy replaces the nodes outright, so both apps are running as brand-new container processes on new hosts — not a warm reload.

**State after the restart**

- **Login works** — `acspeed_probe_71cfef81` authenticates and returns `role: admin`, `isAdmin: true`.
- **Pageview still counted** — `{"pageviews":1,"visitors":1,"visits":1}`, identical to the reading I took immediately before the restart. This one is the real test: my earlier restart in this session happened before any pageview existed, so it couldn't have proven this. The verification's pageview was already in the database this time, and it came through intact.
- **Website still owned by that account** — `acspeed-site-71cfef81` / id `9bc3bd10-890d-4c87-8a27-b69a063e5943`, domain unchanged.
- **Site B still serves the tracking tag** with the same website id.

**Why the storage is durable.** This is by design from the first step, not a retrofit: nothing lives inside a container. All umami state — users, websites, sessions, pageview events — is in a managed RDS PostgreSQL instance (`umami-acs0080e010-db`, `db.t4g.micro`, gp3, automated backups enabled) with its own independent lifecycle. The containers are stateless: umami holds only a connection string, and site B reconstructs its three files from an environment variable at boot. So container replacement destroys no data, and the database itself is a managed instance whose storage persists across reboot.

I generated no traffic during this step — the only requests were umami's authenticated dashboard API and a raw `curl` of site B's HTML, which doesn't execute the tracker.
